qs.q: A 4-year-old child is diagnosed with isolated mild pulmonary valve stenosis during an evaluation for a murmur. Which management strategy is most appropriate?
o: Administration of daily prophylactic oral diuretics
Conservative observation with routine clinical follow-up
Immediate surgical replacement of the pulmonary valve
qs.e: Mild pulmonary stenosis is hemodynamically insignificant and managed conservatively with clinical observation. Invasive interventions like balloon valvuloplasty are reserved for moderate to severe cases.

faq.a: Because the obstruction does not initially cause right‑to‑left shunt; cyanosis appears only when the gradient becomes critical.
faq.q: Why is pulmonary valve stenosis called an acyanotic lesion?

faq.a: Yes, most mild lesions are observed with periodic echo; intervention is reserved for progression or symptoms.
faq.q: Can a child with mild PVS be managed without intervention?

faq.a: It is less invasive, can be done under local anaesthesia, and has lower morbidity in low‑resource settings.
faq.q: What is the main advantage of balloon valvuloplasty over surgery?

exam: A 6‑month‑old infant presents with a harsh systolic murmur and failure to thrive – what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Perform Doppler echocardiography to measure the RV‑PA gradient; it determines severity and need for intervention.

Explain how you would differentiate pulmonary valve stenosis from tetralogy of Fallot on bedside examination. — Look for a single S2 and a harsh murmur in TOF; PVS has a normal S2 and a systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border.

A child with known severe PVS becomes cyanotic after a viral illness – what complication should you suspect? — Acute RV failure or development of a right‑to‑left shunt (e.g., patent ductus arteriosus) causing cyanosis.
Why is balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty preferred as first‑line therapy in moderate PVS? — It directly relieves the obstruction, has high success (> 90 %), and avoids cardiopulmonary bypass.
List three contraindications to balloon valvuloplasty in PVS. — Dysplastic valve with heavy calcification, severe RV dysfunction, or associated large ventricular septal defect requiring surgery.
What ECG changes would support the diagnosis of severe PVS? — Right‑axis deviation and tall R waves in V1‑V2 indicating RV hypertrophy.

During follow‑up, an echo shows a residual gradient of 30 mmHg after valvuloplasty – what does this mean for the patient? — Residual mild obstruction; continue observation, intervene only if gradient rises or symptoms develop.
How does Noonan syndrome influence the management of pulmonary valve stenosis? — Dysplastic valve may be less amenable to balloon; surgical options and genetic counselling are considered.
ai.title: Pulmonary Valve Stenosis
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Pulmonary valve stenosis (PVS) is a congenital obstruction of right‑ventricular outflow that limits blood flow to the lungs. Severity ranges from mild, asymptomatic lesions to critical obstruction causing cyanosis and heart failure.

b: Diagnosed by auscultation (harsh systolic ejection murmur, possible RV heave) and imaging.
Echocardiography is the gold‑standard for confirming valve anatomy and measuring gradient.
sections.p: PVS is a narrowing of the pulmonary valve or infundibulum that creates a pressure gradient between the right ventricle (RV) and pulmonary artery.

t.b: What is the severity? – Peak instantaneous gradient ≥ 64 mmHg = severe; 36‑64 mmHg = moderate; <36 mmHg = mild.
What does it show? – RV enlargement, decreased pulmonary vascular markings in severe cases.
What does it reveal? – Right‑axis deviation, RV hypertrophy; helps when echo not possible.

b: Mild: gradient < 36 mmHg, no symptoms.
Moderate: gradient 36‑64 mmHg, may have exertional dyspnoea.
Severe: gradient ≥ 64 mmHg, RV hypertrophy, possible cyanosis.
sections.p: Severity is staged by the peak systolic gradient measured on Doppler echo and by clinical impact.

b: Isolated congenital dysplastic valve (most common).
Noonan syndrome – associated dysplastic valve.
Rheumatic heart disease – can involve the pulmonary valve, especially in endemic regions.
Infective endocarditis (HIV, malaria‑related bacteremia) – may cause valve thickening.
Maternal drug exposure (e.g., carbimazole) – reported in some series.
sections.p: Most cases are isolated congenital dysplasia; secondary causes are rare but important in low‑resource settings.

b: Mild: often incidental murmur, normal growth.
Moderate: exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, poor weight gain.
Severe/critical: cyanosis, syncope, tachypnoea, hepatomegaly, RV failure signs.
sections.p: Presentation depends on severity and age.

b: Echocardiography – valve morphology, gradient, RV size.
ECG – RV hypertrophy, axis deviation.
Chest X‑ray – RV enlargement, pulmonary vascularity.
Pulse oximetry – detects cyanosis in critical lesions.
sections.p: Focused investigations confirm diagnosis, assess severity, and look for associated lesions.

t.b: What does it answer? – Direct pressure measurement; guides balloon valvuloplasty planning.
Why needed? – To prepare for possible transfusion during intervention.

b: Severe gradient (≥ 64 mmHg) with symptoms.
Cyanosis or drop in oxygen saturation < 85 %.
Signs of RV failure: hepatomegaly, peripheral edema, tachycardia.
Syncope or presyncope on exertion.
sections.p: Identify patients who need urgent referral or intervention.

b: Balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty (BPV) – first‑line for moderate‑to‑severe lesions; avoids open surgery.
Surgical valvotomy or replacement – reserved for failed BPV or dysplastic valves unsuitable for balloon.
Supportive care: diuretics for RV failure, oxygen for cyanosis, treat associated infections (e.g., antibiotics for endocarditis).
Avoid ACE inhibitors or beta‑blockers as primary therapy; they do not relieve obstruction and may worsen RV output.
sections.p: Treatment follows a step‑wise approach: stabilise, relieve obstruction, and monitor.

b: Echocardiography at 6 months post‑BPV, then annually if stable.
Monitor growth, exercise tolerance, and oxygen saturation.
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce pulmonary infections that stress the RV.
Genetic counselling for families with Noonan syndrome or other hereditary patterns.
Aortic stenosis – systolic ejection murmur radiates to carotids, not left upper sternal border.
Tetralogy of Fallot – includes overriding aorta and VSD; cyanosis present early.
Pulmonary hypertension – loud P2, not a valve gradient.
sections.p: Conditions that produce a similar murmur or RV pressure overload.

b: Mild gradient on echo may underestimate severity if Doppler angle is off; consider clinical picture.
Normal chest X‑ray does not rule out severe stenosis; RV enlargement may be subtle.
ECG may be normal in early disease; do not rely on it alone.
sections.p: Pitfalls in interpretation, especially where resources are limited.

whenToSeekHelp: New cyanosis or oxygen saturation < 85 % at rest.
Syncope, presyncope, or severe dyspnoea on minimal activity.
Rapid weight loss, hepatomegaly, or peripheral edema suggesting RV failure.
